Die Serienkomposition übernimmt Naoki Tozuka (I Was Reincarnated as the 7th Prince, Meiji Gekken: 1874), während das Charakterdesign von Naru Nishikiori (I Was Reincarnated as the 7th Prince) stammt.

Die Geschichte startete im Juni 2020 zunächst als Web Novel auf Shōsetsuka ni Narō. Kodansha begann das Werk mit Illustrationen von Pukyunosuke im Januar 2021 als Printausgabe zu veröffentlichen und umfasst derzeit 7 Bände.

Die gleichnamige Manga-Adaption wird von Matsu umgesetzt und läuft seit April 2021 in der Palcy App von Kodansha. Das 13 Band erscheint am 30. Juli in Japan. Eine englische Ausgabe erscheint bei Kodansha USA Publishing, während hierzulande die Reihe nicht auf Deutsch erhältlich ist.

📜 Beschreibung 》
Seit ihrer Kindheit schützt Eliane das Königreich Belkheim als wahre Heilige. Mit ihren Gebeten hält sie Monster fern und sorgt für reiche Ernten, doch ihr Einsatz wird mit Verrat belohnt. Als eine falsche Heilige den leichtgläubigen Prinzen täuscht, löst dieser die Verlobung und verbannt Eliane aus dem Land. Ohne Geld und Heimat macht sie sich auf den Weg ins Nachbarkönigreich, um dort endlich ein stilles Leben als einfache Bürgerin zu führen. Doch eine unerwartete Begegnung bringt ihre neuen Pläne schon bald ins Wanken.

»Eliane« von Matsumi Tazawa
Die wahre Heilige, die den Segen der Göttin erhalten hat. Im Königreich Belkaim stützte sie das Land mit ihrer Kraft, bis ihr Verlobter Claude plötzlich die Verlobung löste und sie aus dem Land verbannte. Eliane ist freundlich, ernsthaft und bescheiden, besitzt aber zugleich eine starke innere Haltung.
»Nigel« von Taku Yashiro
Der erste Prinz von Lynchigham. Nachdem er im Kampf gegen Monster verletzt wurde, wird er von Eliane gerettet. Nigel ist höflich, pflichtbewusst und ein sanfter junger Mann. Da er allen Menschen ohne Vorurteile begegnet, genießt er großes Vertrauen bei den Bürgern, zeigt aber gelegentlich auch eine etwas tollpatschige Seite.

🔋 MIT just published the most comprehensive EV emissions study yet, analyzing every US zip code with real driving data.

Battery EVs cut lifetime emissions 40-60% vs gas cars in most locations. Even on the dirtiest grid in the country, they still come out ahead. The study used DOE's GREET lifecycle model, which already includes battery manufacturing. So the "but what about making the batteries?" question is answered: building an EV produces 50-80% more CO2 upfront, but it pays that back over the vehicle's life.

Your driving habits matter as much as where you live. High mileage, city driving, and larger vehicles all boost the EV advantage. Cold weather cuts efficiency on a frigid night but barely dents annual savings.

The "who benefits from the doubt?" question has a paper trail. The API has run anti-EV messaging since 1967. Koch-funded groups planned $10M/year campaigns. AFPM dropped $10M+ on "Don't Ban Our Cars" ads in 2024 swing states.

The key is to optimize the cost-to-outcome frontier in real world context. In practical terms, that means using the right model for each task, and optimizing the context, skills, tools, and agent harness around it.
This is the motivation behind our MAI model family. These models have been built ground up with clean data lineage and optimized for learning transfer from generalist to specialized skills in enterprise RLEs. We continue to make rapid progress in this pursuit.

We can now take saturated frontier capabilities and deliver them at scale and at lower cost through models optimized for high-usage products, while continuing to use frontier models for frontier needs.
We are proving this out across our first party products, and thereby creating a template for every other Al native, Saas, or Enterprise company out there.
In our products, frontier models from OpenAl and Anthropic are part of the orchestration system alongside MAI. But the model is only one part of the hill-climbing system. Harness, memory, context, tools, skills, user interactions, etc. all shape the evals and performance of these agentic systems.

continue to hill climb even when any given model has been removed.
Therefore we build RLEs where models learn inside the product system and are rewarded for completing the tasks customers actually care about. We train models against the actual product harness, interactions, and outcomes they will encounter. And strategically ensure that the harness, memory, context, skills are externalized outside of the model.
Product-specific evals and model independence give us the control and a direct hill to climb, and to keep refining until we reach the right quality-cost target. We are now seeing MAI models outperform general-purpose frontier models in many use cases while using a fraction of the tokens.

AI Overview
A diesel delete involves removing emissions components like the DPF, EGR, and DEF systems, and installing custom tuning. While done to improve fuel economy and prevent soot clogs, it is a federal crime under the Clean Air Act to tamper with emissions. Kits often range from $2,000 to $6,000+. 
The Mechanics: What is a Delete?
A delete kit physically replaces or bypasses specific emissions hardware with aftermarket pipes and block-off plates: 

    DPF (Diesel Particulate Filter): Replaced with a straight pipe to stop the restrictive regeneration (regen) cycles that burn fuel to clean the filter.
    EGR (Exhaust Gas Recirculation): Replaced with block-off plates to stop hot, sooty exhaust from being routed back into the engine.
    DEF (Diesel Exhaust Fluid): Deactivated electronically to prevent urea-related derates, though the physical tank can sometimes remain.
     

Performance and Cost
While deleting can yield horsepower gains of 40-120 HP and a 3-5 MPG increase, the upfront costs are substantial. 

    Parts and Tuning: Kits typically range from $2,800 to over $5,800, depending on the truck and hardware.
    Labor: Professional installation can easily cost hundreds to thousands of dollars if you are not doing the work yourself.
    Warranty: Modifying the ECM and removing hardware will instantly void your factory powertrain and drivetrain warranties. 

Legal Risks and Enforcement
The federal Clean Air Act prohibits the removal or disabling of emissions control devices on any vehicle originally manufactured with them. While the Department of Justice announced it will no longer criminally prosecute owners for emissions tampering, heavy civil fines are still actively enforced. Additionally, state and county environmental boards can pursue civil penalties, and many shops refuse to work on deleted vehicles.
